Let the vertices be fixed as \(\{1,\dots,8\}\). I used a direct finite enumeration from the definitions.

Encode each edge of \(K_8\) as a bit. There are

\[
7\cdot5\cdot3\cdot1=105
\]

perfect matchings. A one-factorization is then an exact partition of the 28 edge-bits into 7 such 4-edge masks. Recursively choosing the least uncovered edge and then one available perfect matching containing it gives every labeled one-factorization exactly once. This gives

\[
6240
\]

labeled one-factorizations.

Now form the graph \(\Gamma\) whose vertices are these 6240 one-factorizations, with an edge between two vertices exactly when the corresponding one-factorizations are orthogonal. A family of pairwise orthogonal one-factorizations is precisely a clique in \(\Gamma\).

The full finite audit of \(\Gamma\) gives the following degree distribution:

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\deg &0&2&4&24&240\\
\#\text{ vertices}&3150&960&1680&420&30
\end{array}
\]

and the common-neighbor distribution over adjacent pairs is

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\#\text{ common neighbors}&0&1&8\\
\#\text{ adjacent pairs}&10920&1920&120
\end{array}
\]

Thus the number of triangles is

\[
\frac{1920\cdot1+120\cdot8}{3}=960.
\]

Every triangle has degree pattern

\[
(2,240,240).
\]

So each triangle contains a vertex of degree \(2\), and its two neighbors are exactly the other two vertices of the triangle. Hence no triangle can be extended to a \(4\)-clique. Therefore the largest possible family size is

\[
m=3.
\]

There are exactly \(960\) triangles in \(\Gamma\), and triangles are exactly unordered families of three pairwise orthogonal one-factorizations, so

\[
N=960.
\]

An explicit attaining triple is given by the following three one-factorizations:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal F_1=&\{12345678,\ 13245768,\ 14235867,\ 15263748,\\
&\qquad 16253847,\ 17283546,\ 18273645\},\\
\mathcal F_2=&\{12364857,\ 13264758,\ 14283756,\ 15273846,\\
&\qquad 16234578,\ 17253468,\ 18243567\},\\
\mathcal F_3=&\{12384567,\ 13274856,\ 14263578,\ 15234768,\\
&\qquad 16283457,\ 17243658,\ 18253746\},
\end{aligned}
\]

where, for example, \(12345678\) means \(\{12,34,56,78\}\). Direct comparison shows every matching from one factorization meets every matching from another in at most one edge.

Therefore the requested ordered pair is

\[
\boxed{(3,960)}.
\]
